warmup.q: You run curl http://example.com/ in a container. The Ethernet frame that carries your GET request has a destination MAC address. Whose network card does that MAC belong to?
options: Your default gateway, the next box on the path
The DNS server that looked up example.com
Nobody's: it is ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff, the broadcast address
warmup.why: A MAC address only means something on one link. Your container can't reach example.com's card directly, so it addresses the frame to the gateway and puts example.com's address in the IP header instead. Every router on the way writes a new Ethernet header for the next link. In the capture in this lesson the destination MAC is 22:d2:d5:a2:32:a3, which belongs to the Docker bridge, the box's gateway.

sections.h: Getting bytes to another machine takes four kinds of address
sections.html:
Here is what curl http://example.com/ wants to send. It is 74 bytes of text:

GET / HTTP/1.1
Host: example.com
User-Agent: curl/8.5.0
Accept: */*

(Each line ends with two invisible characters, a carriage return and a line feed, and an empty line ends the request.) Curl's job is to get those bytes to a program on a machine it only knows by name. Try to design that from nothing, and four problems turn up, one after another.

Start with the simplest case: two computers joined by one cable. Each has a network card, the hardware that turns bytes into signals on the wire and back. Your machine pushes the 74 bytes down the cable and the other card receives them. No addresses needed.

Put a third computer on the same cable, or on the same Wi-Fi network, and that stops working. Every card now hears every transmission, so each card needs a name, and each chunk of data needs a label saying which card it is for. That name is a MAC address: six bytes given to each card, written like 22:d2:d5:a2:32:a3. A chunk of data labelled this way is a frame, and the cards that can hear each other directly form one link. Moving frames across one link is the job of the link layer. Ethernet is the standard for wired links, and Wi-Fi behaves the same way as far as your software can tell.

Now the server isn't on your link at all. example.com sits in a data centre behind dozens of other links. Its card can't hear yours, and nobody could keep a list of every card on the planet. So a second kind of address works across links: an IP address, four bytes written like 104.20.23.154. Between links sit routers, machines with a card on two or more links. A router reads the destination IP address of whatever arrives, picks the next link that leads closer to it, and passes it on. Your machine only needs to know one router, its default gateway, and hands it everything that isn't on its own link. This is the internet layer, and a chunk of data with IP addresses on it is a packet.

Reaching the right machine still isn't enough. The server runs many programs, and bytes for the web server must not end up in the database. So each program that talks on the network gets a number, a port: 80 for plain web traffic, 443 for HTTPS, the encrypted kind. This layer, the transport layer, also has to cope with the network's habits: packets get lost, duplicated and reordered, and IP fixes none of that. TCP, the transport protocol curl uses, numbers every byte, resends what goes missing and hands the receiver the bytes in their original order.

Last, people type names, not numbers. Something must turn example.com into 104.20.23.154 before anything else can happen. That is DNS, a lookup service that is itself just another program on the network. It lives at the top of the stack, in the application layer, next to HTTP.

So the software that moves your request is four layers, each answering one question with its own kind of address:

Layer Question it answers Protocol here Addresses in this request
Application what to say, to which name HTTP, DNS example.com
Transport which program, in what order TCP port 57236 to port 80
Internet which machine, across links IP 172.20.0.2 to 104.20.23.154
Link which card on this link Ethernet b6:99:4a:b0:80:7f to 22:d2:d5:a2:32:a3

Keep this table in your head for the whole track: every later lesson zooms into one row of it. You will also hear the rows called by numbers from an older model, OSI: L2 for the link, L3 for IP, L4 for TCP and L7 for the application. An "L4 load balancer" forwards TCP connections without reading them; an "L7 load balancer" reads the HTTP request to choose a server.

Two entries surprise most people. The destination MAC isn't the server's: it belongs to the gateway, the next card on your own link. And curl never chose port 57236. The kernel, the core of the operating system that owns the network card, picked a free port for this one connection. The Try it shows all four pairs for a live connection.

try.title: Find all four addresses
steps: Start the lab box from the labs folder: docker compose -f env/labbox.yml run --rm box. You get a root shell on Ubuntu with every tool this track uses.

Run the commands below one at a time. The exec 3<>/dev/tcp/... line is a bash trick: it opens a TCP connection and keeps it open as file descriptor 3 (a numbered handle the shell holds), so ss, Linux's tool for listing sockets, has something to show.
Match each line of output to a row of the table: the name and its IP, your IP, your port and theirs, and the gateway's MAC.
On a Mac there is no ip or ss. Use ifconfig en0 for your IP and MAC, netstat -rn -f inet for the gateway, arp -an for the MACs your Mac has learned, and lsof -nP -iTCP for open connections.

code.title: in the lab box
code.html: getent ahostsv4 example.com | head -1 # name -> IP, through the resolver ip -br -4 addr show eth0 # your IP and prefix ip -br link show eth0 # your MAC ip route show default # where packets for the internet go exec 3<>/dev/tcp/example.com/80 # open a TCP connection and keep it ss -tn dst :80 # both ends of it: IP and port ip neigh show # the gateway's MAC, learned just now exec 3>&- # close the connection

sections.h: Encapsulation: each layer wraps the one above it
sections.html:
The four layers don't send four separate messages. They nest. When curl writes its 74 bytes into a socket (the kernel's handle for one network conversation, which a program reads and writes much like a file), the bytes travel down the stack inside the kernel, and each layer puts its own header in front: a few bytes holding that layer's addresses and bookkeeping.

  • TCP adds 32 bytes: the two ports, the numbers it uses to keep bytes in order, some flags and a few options. 74 bytes become 106.
  • IP adds 20 bytes: the two IP addresses, a TTL (time to live) counter that every router lowers by one so that a packet caught in a loop dies at zero, a protocol number, and a checksum (a number computed from the header's bytes, so a receiver can spot damage). 106 become 126.
  • Ethernet adds 14 bytes: the two MAC addresses and a type field. 126 become 140, and the network card sends those 140 bytes as one frame.

This is encapsulation: each layer treats whatever the layer above handed it as an opaque payload and wraps it in its own envelope.

At the receiving end the kernel runs the same steps backwards, and that is where the last field of each header earns its place. Every header says what is inside it. Ethernet's type field, the EtherType, is 0x0800: an IPv4 packet follows (IPv4 is the version of IP with 4-byte addresses; lesson 5 covers IPv6). IP's protocol field is 6: a TCP segment follows (17 would mean UDP, a simpler transport that doesn't resend or reorder). TCP's destination port is 80, which picks the program. The kernel follows those three fields, one per layer, and hands the web server exactly the 74 bytes curl wrote. It never guesses from the content.

Routers in the middle open only the outer envelope. A router takes off the Ethernet header, reads the destination IP address, lowers the TTL by one, and wraps the packet in a new Ethernet header addressed to the next card on the next link. It never reads TCP or HTTP. That is why the MAC addresses change at every hop while the IP addresses and ports arrive untouched. It is also why the layers can change independently: Ethernet doesn't know it carries HTTP, and HTTP doesn't know whether it crossed a cable, Wi-Fi or a mobile network.

The unit at each layer has its own name. HTTP sends a message, TCP a segment, IP a packet and Ethernet a frame, which is everything on the wire, headers included. Step through the real 140-byte frame from the Try it below: built in the lab box, passed on by one router, and taken apart at the server.

video.title: From a URL to bytes on the wire

sections.h: Three waits happen before your request is even sent
sections.html:
Go back to the moment you press Enter, before any of those 140 bytes exist. Three things have to happen first, and each costs at least one round trip: the time for a message to reach the other end and for an answer to come back. Inside one data centre a round trip takes well under a millisecond. Between the east and west coasts of the US it is about 70 ms. From the lab box to example.com's nearest server it was about 9 ms.

First comes DNS. The kernel can't fill in an IP header without an IP address, so curl asks a resolver, a server whose job is to look names up, what example.com is. The question and its answer are one round trip, more if the resolver has to ask other servers.

Second, the TCP handshake. Before TCP can number and resend bytes, both sides must agree where the numbering starts and know that the other side is there. The client sends a SYN (synchronize), the server answers with a SYN-ACK (synchronize, acknowledged), and the client confirms with an ACK. The request can travel with that last step, so the handshake costs one round trip.

Third, for HTTPS, TLS. The two sides agree on encryption keys, and the client checks the server's certificate, its proof that it really is example.com. With TLS 1.3 that takes one more round trip, plus some computing time.

Only then does the request leave, and the first byte of the answer arrives one round trip, plus the server's own work, later. curl can time every step. Each number is seconds since curl started, so it includes the steps before it:

dns 0.012801  connect 0.021870  tls 0.038789  first byte 0.052085  total 0.052110
Step Done at Took What happened
DNS 12.8 ms 12.8 ms a resolver turned example.com into an IP address
TCP connect 21.9 ms 9.1 ms SYN out, SYN-ACK back: one round trip
TLS 38.8 ms 16.9 ms keys and certificate: a round trip plus crypto work
First byte 52.1 ms 13.3 ms the request went out and the answer started coming back

Three quarters of the total had passed before a single byte of HTTP left the machine.

The fix is to pay for setup once. Ask curl for the same URL twice in one run, and the second transfer reuses the connection the first one opened:

dns 0.002230  connect 0.011069  tls 0.028304  first byte 0.041567  total 0.041588
dns 0.000007  connect 0.000000  tls 0.000000  first byte 0.014657  total 0.014677

No lookup, no handshake, no TLS: 14.7 ms instead of 41.6. That gap is the reason connection pools exist. A pool keeps connections open between requests, so only the first request on each connection pays for DNS, TCP and TLS. Lesson 7 of this track opens up the TCP handshake, lesson 9 DNS and lesson 10 TLS. For now it's enough to know the three waits are there.

sections.h: Packets on the wire, a byte stream in your code
sections.html:
So far the request fit in one frame. A 1 MB response from a ledger service doesn't, because every link limits the size of a frame.

The limit exists because one frame holds the wire, or the radio channel, for as long as it takes to send, and because every card must have buffer space for the largest frame it might receive. Ethernet settled on at most 1,500 bytes of payload per frame. That number is the link's MTU (maximum transmission unit), and it hasn't changed on ordinary Ethernet since the 1980s.

So something must cut large data into pieces that fit, and that is TCP's job. Take the 20 bytes of IP header and the 20 bytes of TCP header off 1,500, and 1,460 bytes of data fit in one segment. TCP announces this number, the MSS (maximum segment size), when it opens a connection; the capture shows mss 1460. Here both sides also switched on TCP timestamps, 12 bytes of options in every segment, so 1,448 bytes of data ride in each full packet. A 1 MB response arrives as about 700 packets.

Your code sees none of them. A program calls write() on a socket with some bytes, and the program at the other end calls read() and gets bytes back. TCP decides where to cut, numbers every byte, resends what gets lost and puts the pieces back in order, so the receiver sees one continuous stream of bytes with no message boundaries in it. One write() of 4,000 bytes can come out as three read()s, and one read() can return the end of one message and the start of the next. That is why every protocol built on TCP marks where its messages end. HTTP does it with a Content-Length header that says how many bytes the body has, or by sending the body in chunks that each start with their length.

The capture of one small curl shows a whole TCP conversation. It is 11 packets for a 74-byte request and a 936-byte answer: three to open the connection (SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK), the request, an acknowledgment of it, the response, an acknowledgment of that, and four to close (each side sends a FIN, for finish, and acknowledges the other's). Only two of the eleven carry any data.

One habit to take from this: when write() returns, the kernel has only copied your bytes into its own buffer. It may not have sent them yet, it can't know whether they arrived, and it certainly can't tell you that the server acted on them. For a payment, only an answer from the server tells you that.

Only two lines carry data. The box's SYN says mss 1460, the Ethernet number. The SYN-ACK says mss 65495, which no Ethernet link has: on Docker Desktop your container's TCP connection ends inside Docker's own network proxy, which opens a second connection from your Mac to the server. It is a first hint that "the other end" of a connection is not always the machine you think.

refs.title: High Performance Browser Networking: Building blocks of TCP

analogy: Sending a request is like posting a letter inside nested envelopes. You write the letter (HTTP). The mailroom puts it in an envelope marked with the department's room number (the port). The post office puts that inside an envelope with the street address (the IP address). A courier sticks on a label that only says which depot to drive to next (the MAC address). At every depot the courier's label is torn off and a new one goes on for the next leg, but the street address stays the same all the way. The analogy breaks in two places: the post office never cuts a long letter into 1,460-byte strips and glues them back together at the other end, and it doesn't notice a lost envelope and send a copy. TCP does both.
world: Your Quarkus payment service calls a card issuer over HTTPS, and the dashboard says the call takes 120 ms. Before you open a ticket with the issuer, split that number the way curl does. When the connection pool is cold, after a deploy or a long quiet period, the first call pays for DNS, a TCP handshake and a TLS handshake: three or more round trips before the authorization request even leaves. If the issuer is 15 ms away, that is 45 ms or more of your 120 that the issuer never sees in its logs. A warm pooled connection pays only for the request. The layers also explain the words in your incident channel: an AWS Network Load Balancer is an L4 balancer that forwards TCP, an Application Load Balancer is L7 and reads your HTTP, and your Kafka clients keep long-lived TCP connections to each broker so that no message pays for setup.
mistake: The common mistake is reading total request time as server time. Someone sees a slow outbound call, raises it with the provider, and the provider's logs show a 20 ms response. The missing time was spent before the request was sent: DNS lookups, TCP handshakes and TLS handshakes on connections that were not reused, usually because the HTTP client was built per request, or the pool closed idle connections between calls. Measure the phases separately (curl -w from the same host, or your HTTP client's connect and TLS timings), and reuse connections: create one HTTP client per target and keep it for the life of the service.

compare.title: The same request, as curl shows it and as the wire carries it

a.label: curl -v
a.title: what the application wrote
a.html:
> GET / HTTP/1.1
> Host: example.com
> User-Agent: curl/8.5.0
> Accept: */*
>

compare.note: Both show the same 74 bytes of HTTP. curl prints them as text lines, prefixed with >. On the wire the same text starts at byte 66 (4745 5420, "GET "), after 66 bytes curl never sees: 14 of Ethernet, 20 of IP and 32 of TCP. The kernel wrote all of those, which is why the lab parses them out of the frame rather than out of curl's output.

steps.say: Take the 140-byte GET frame from the Try it. The first 14 bytes are the Ethernet header: destination MAC, source MAC, EtherType. Destination comes first so a switch can decide where to send the frame as soon as the first bytes arrive.
steps.code:
0x0000:  22d2 d5a2 32a3 b699 4ab0 807f 0800 4500

22 d2 d5 a2 32 a3   destination MAC 22:d2:d5:a2:32:a3 (the gateway)
b6 99 4a b0 80 7f   source MAC b6:99:4a:b0:80:7f (the lab box)
08 00               EtherType 0x0800: an IPv4 packet follows

steps.say: IP starts at byte 14. Its first byte holds two numbers: the high half is the version, 4, and the low half is the header length in 4-byte words, 5, so 20 bytes. The rest are fixed fields.
steps.code:
45         version 4, header length 5 x 4 = 20 bytes
00         type of service
00 7e      total length 126 = 20 IP + 32 TCP + 74 data
43 d4      identification
40 00      flags: Don't Fragment set; fragment offset 0
40         TTL 64
06         protocol 6: TCP follows
ca e1      header checksum
ac 14 00 02  source 172.20.0.2
68 14 17 9a  destination 104.20.23.154

steps.say: TCP starts at byte 14 + 20 = 34 (0x22). Ports first, then the two 32-bit counters. The high half of byte 46 is TCP's header length in words: 8, so 32 bytes, of which 12 are options. Byte 47 holds the flags.
steps.code:
df 94        source port 57236
00 50        destination port 80
b4 a1 85 7c  sequence number 3030484348
b1 90 d4 2b  acknowledgment number 2979058731
80           header length 8 x 4 = 32 bytes
18           flags 0x18 = PSH (0x08) + ACK (0x10)
01 f6        window 502
2c 35        checksum (left for the card to finish, see Go deeper)
00 00        urgent pointer
01 01 08 0a 3c5b486f a9c964c0   options: NOP, NOP, timestamps

steps.say: The application data starts at 14 + 20 + 32 = 66, which is 0x42. That is where 47 45 54 20 spells GET. From there to the end, 74 bytes, is exactly what curl wrote. The lab asks you to write this walk as code.

lab.title: Peel a captured frame layer by layer
steps: Run the tests once from the labs folder. All 12 fail with NotImplementedError. Open src/test/resources/sfz/net/l01/http-get.txt: it is the frame from the Try it, exactly as tcpdump printed it, and the tests read it from there.
Read Layers.kt. The classes are finished, and each field's comment says which bytes it comes from.
In Decapsulate.kt, write parseEthernet, then parseIpv4, then parseTcp. Wrap the array in a ByteBuffer and widen every number before you store it.
Write ipv4Checksum and check it against cae1, the value the kernel wrote into the captured header.
Write decapsulate. It checks each layer's "what's inside" field (EtherType, then protocol) before it hands the payload to the next parser. Run the tests until all 12 pass.
hints: ByteBuffer.wrap(bytes).getShort(12).toInt() and 0xffff reads bytes 12 and 13 as an unsigned number. Without the and 0xffff, port 57236 comes out negative.
The sequence numbers are above 2^31. Read them with getInt(4).toLong() and 0xffffffffL.
IHL is bytes[0].toInt() and 0x0f, counted in 4-byte words. TCP's header length is the high half of byte 12: (bytes[12].toInt() and 0xff) shr 4, also in words.
Cut the IP payload with copyOfRange(headerLength, totalLength), not up to size: one test adds Ethernet padding to the frame.
For the checksum, add each 16-bit word into a Long, skipping the word at index 10. Fold with while (sum shr 16 != 0L) sum = (sum and 0xffff) + (sum shr 16) and return sum.inv().toInt() and 0xffff.

drill.title: Draw the frame from memory
drill.prompt: Without looking back, write the layers of the GET frame from the outside in. For each one give its header size in this capture, the field that says what's inside it, and the pair of addresses it carries. Then add up the sizes and check against the answer.

answer.html:
Ethernet  14 bytes   EtherType 0x0800 = IPv4   MACs   b6:99:4a:b0:80:7f > 22:d2:d5:a2:32:a3 (box > gateway)
IPv4      20 bytes   protocol 6 = TCP          IPs    172.20.0.2 > 104.20.23.154
TCP       32 bytes   port 80 = the web server  ports  57236 > 80
HTTP      74 bytes                             name   Host: example.com
total    140 bytes on the wire, plus a 4-byte FCS the card adds and tcpdump never shows

recap: A request waits for DNS, the TCP handshake and TLS before it is even sent. curl -w times each step, and a reused connection skips all three.
Four layers, four addresses: a name for people, a port for the program, an IP address for the machine and a MAC address for the next box on the wire.
MAC addresses are rewritten at every router. IP addresses and ports travel end to end, until a NAT rewrites them (lesson 3).
Each layer adds a header on the way down and removes it on the way up. EtherType, IP protocol and port say what's inside, so the receiver never guesses.
Ethernet's MTU is 1,500 bytes, so TCP cuts your stream into segments of at most 1,460 bytes of data. Your code sees a byte stream, never packets.

explain.prompt: A colleague asks why the frame carrying their HTTP request has the gateway's MAC address as its destination, not the server's. Explain it in your own words, and say where the server's address is.
explain.answer: A MAC address only works on one link: it tells the switch or the Wi-Fi which card on this wire should take the frame. The server is many links away, so my machine can't address its card. The kernel sees that the destination IP is not on the local network, so it hands the frame to the default gateway by putting the gateway's MAC in the Ethernet header. The server's address is in the IP header, and it stays there all the way. Every router on the path takes the Ethernet header off, reads the IP header to choose the next hop, and wraps the packet in a new Ethernet header for the next link.

deeper.html:
Why tcpdump calls your TCP checksum wrong. Run tcpdump -vv -r /tmp/get.pcap and every packet the box sent shows something like cksum 0x2c35 (incorrect -> 0x85e6). Nothing is broken. Linux leaves the TCP checksum for the network card to finish (checksum offload), and tcpdump copies the packet before that happens. ethtool -k eth0 | grep checksum in the lab box shows tx-checksumming: on. The IP header checksum is different: the kernel computes it itself, which is why the lab can check it against the capture.

Segments bigger than the MTU. During a big download you may see TCP segments of 20,000 bytes or more in tcpdump. That is segmentation offload: the kernel hands the card (or the virtual device) one large segment, which gets cut into MTU-sized frames below the point where tcpdump watches. The wire never carries more than 1,500 bytes of payload per frame. ethtool -k eth0 | grep segmentation shows it switched on in the lab box.

Where the OSI model went. OSI was designed from the late 1970s as a complete protocol suite, and it lost to TCP/IP. Its numbering stuck because textbooks taught it everywhere. Its session and presentation layers (5 and 6) have no separate protocol in the internet stack: TLS is sometimes called layer 6, but it runs inside the application. QUIC, the transport under HTTP/3, folds reliability, encryption and multiplexing into one protocol on top of UDP and fits no layer diagram. Use the numbers as vocabulary and no further.

The checksum at the end of every frame. Each Ethernet frame ends with a 4-byte CRC-32, the frame check sequence. The receiving card computes it, drops frames that don't match and strips it before the kernel sees the frame, so captures almost never show it. A climbing RX errors count in ip -s link show eth0 is how a bad cable or a noisy Wi-Fi link shows up.
